title: Republicans Spend Millions Defending Districts Redrawn to Favor Them
excerpt: Fifteen House districts were redrawn to give Republicans an edge before November 3. With a week left, most are toss-ups, Texas Latino voters are shifting, and the party is spending heavily to hold its own map.
body:
• Republicans redrew 15 House districts to favour them ahead of the November 3, 2026 midterms, but only five are rated likely or solid Republican by the Cook Political Report.
  • North Carolina's 1st District, redrawn so Trump would have won it by over 11 points in 2024, is now a toss-up and has drawn more than $42 million in ad spending from September 1 to Election Day.
  • In Texas, polls show Latino voters leaning Democratic by about 2-to-1, undermining maps drawn on the assumption that Trump's 2024 support among them would hold.
  • Democrats need a net gain of just four seats to take the House — Indian-American voters and candidates in redrawn suburban districts could help decide several of the toss-ups.

Starting last year, President Trump and his political team pressed Republican-led states to redraw congressional district lines to favour Republicans. The aim was a firewall against the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses for the president's party. Eight days before the November 3 election, that firewall is consuming money instead of saving it.

"It just has not turned out that way," said Nathan Gonzales, editor of Inside Elections, in NPR's reporting. Republicans gained an advantage in 15 districts nationwide, Gonzales said, but some that were supposed to be easy victories are not turning out that way, and the party is pouring millions into districts that were meant to be safe.

"It just has not turned out that way."

— Nathan Gonzales, editor of Inside Elections, to NPR

North Carolina Shows the Problem

North Carolina's 1st District was aggressively redrawn late last year to make it reliably Republican. Under the new lines, Trump would have won it by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. It is now widely considered a toss-up. The race between Republican Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel who lost in the district two years ago, and Democratic Rep. Don Davis has become one of the most expensive House contests in the country, with more than $42 million spent on advertising between September 1 and Election Day, according to an NPR analysis of AdImpact data.

Davis, whose home county was drawn out of the district, has campaigned in six new counties and focused on affordability. Republicans and Democrats alike acknowledge he is a formidable campaigner. Trump himself headlined a rally in eastern North Carolina and, at House Speaker Mike Johnson's request, gave Buckhout a special call-out because her race would be close. Two Florida districts redrawn to remove Democratic incumbents are nearing a combined $90 million in ad spending, NPR reported.

Texas: Maps Drawn on a 2024 electorate

Texas was the centrepiece of the strategy: the legislature aimed to flip five Democratic seats. But as USA Today reported, the new Latino-heavy seats were drawn assuming Trump's record 2024 performance among Hispanic voters — 55% of the Texas Latino vote — would repeat. Recent polling points the other way: a Latino Community Foundation poll found likely Texas voters planning to vote Democratic for Congress by a 2-to-1 margin, and a Cook Political Report-TelevisaUnivision survey found a similar 2-to-1 Democratic lead among Hispanic voters.

Cook now rates Texas's 15th and 34th districts as toss-ups and the 28th as leaning Democratic, while Republicans remain likely to flip the redrawn 9th, 32nd and 35th. Even a Republican strategist in Texas called picking up all five seats "unrealistic," expecting two or three. A Republican strategist involved in midterm races told NPR that "redistricting creates new battlefields, it doesn't create outcomes."

What to Watch on November 3

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the House. If redrawn districts in North Carolina, Texas and Florida stay competitive to the end, Republicans must spend to defend the map they drew while also holding vulnerable incumbents elsewhere. The result will be decided less by the lines than by turnout among the voters the lines assumed — including Latino and suburban voters whose shift since 2024 is the central fact of this midterm cycle.
